In scientific tasks where embedding-based tool--task alignment is low, dynamically pruning the available tool set to retain only those tools whose descriptions exceed a task-specific similarity threshold will reduce distractor-induced failures and yield higher pass@5 scores than exposing the agent to the full static tool set.

Dynamic, subgoal-specific tool provisioning guided by thresholded embedding similarity between available tools and the agent’s current intermediate objective will outperform static, task-level tool provisioning in complex scientific environments, particularly when the base model lacks specialized domain knowledge.

Dynamically pruning the toolset presented to a scientific agent so that only the tools whose descriptions have the highest embedding similarity to the task prompt are available will improve pass@5 success and reduce wasted tool calls in low task–tool alignment environments more than switching to a ReAct framework or increasing tool-description verbosity.
